title: Tested in the Wilderness, Light in Galilee
summary: Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and is tempted by the devil three times, answering each temptation with words from Deuteronomy. After John's arrest Jesus moves to Capernaum in Galilee, fulfilling Isaiah's promise of light for Galilee of the Gentiles, and begins to preach that the kingdom of heaven is near. He calls four fishermen to follow him and travels through Galilee teaching, preaching, and healing, as crowds gather from every direction.
story: At his baptism Jesus was declared God's beloved Son. Now that sonship is tested. Israel, called God's son at the exodus, passed through the sea and then spent forty years in the wilderness, where it grumbled for bread, put God to the test, and turned to idols. Jesus passes through the water and spends forty days in the wilderness, and where Israel failed he remains faithful, answering the devil with the very words Moses spoke to Israel about those wilderness years. Having won that contest, he begins his public ministry. The second half of the chapter moves from the lonely wilderness to the crowded lakeshore, and the pattern of his ministry is set: preaching the kingdom, calling disciples, and healing. The Sermon on the Mount follows immediately.
historical:
Jesus' ministry began after John the Baptist was imprisoned by Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea for Rome from 4 BC to AD 39. Jesus made his base in Capernaum, a lakeside fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, near a main road. Excavations there have uncovered a village of basalt houses and the remains of a later synagogue built over earlier foundations, and a first-century house that early Christians venerated as Peter's. In 1986 a fishing boat from about the first century was found in the mud near the lake's shore, giving a picture of the kind of boat the brothers worked from.

The quotation from Isaiah recalls an older history. Zebulun and Naphtali, the tribal territories around the Sea of Galilee, were the first parts of Israel conquered by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29), and Isaiah spoke of that darkened region as the first to see the light. By Jesus' day Galilee was largely Jewish again, but it was surrounded by Gentile territory and carried the old name Galilee of the Gentiles. The Decapolis in verse 25 was a league of Greek cities mostly east of the Jordan.
cultural:
Forty days of fasting recalled Moses, who fasted forty days on Mount Sinai (Exodus 34:28), and Elijah, who traveled forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). The pinnacle of the temple was probably a high point on the temple's outer walls, perhaps the southeast corner overlooking the Kidron Valley. The devil's offer of all the kingdoms of the world echoes the reality of Roman imperial power, which claimed exactly that dominion.

In Jesus' world, students usually chose their teacher and attached themselves to him to learn the law. Jesus reverses this: he chooses and calls. Fishing on the Sea of Galilee was a significant trade, with nets cast from the shore or from boats and the catch often salted and sold. James and John leaving their father Zebedee in the boat was a serious break, since sons normally worked in and inherited the family business and owed their fathers honor and support. Synagogues, local gatherings for prayer and the reading and teaching of Scripture, were found throughout Galilee, and visiting teachers could be invited to speak.
literary: The temptation scene (verses 1 to 11) is a structured contest in three rounds, each beginning with the devil's challenge and ending with Jesus' reply, it is written. All three replies come from Deuteronomy 6 to 8, Moses' reflections on Israel's time in the wilderness. In the first two the devil begins If You are the Son of God, questioning what the Father has just declared; in the third he drops the pretense and asks for worship. The devil also quotes Scripture (Psalm 91:11-12), showing that citing the Bible is not the same as obeying it. The second half (verses 12 to 25) is a transition narrative with a fulfillment quotation (Isaiah 9:1-2), a summary of Jesus' preaching, a call story told twice in parallel, and a summary of his ministry. Verse 23 is nearly repeated in 9:35, framing the teaching of chapters 5 to 7 and the healings of chapters 8 and 9 between them.

outline.t: The first test: stones into bread
The second test: the pinnacle of the temple
The third test: all the kingdoms of the world
Jesus moves to Capernaum and preaches the kingdom
The call of the first disciples
Teaching, preaching, and healing throughout Galilee

doctrines.note: Jesus answers every temptation with Scripture, treating God's word as the bread he lives by. The devil's misuse of Psalm 91 shows that Scripture must be read in its sense and not bent to serve a purpose it was never given.
Jesus refuses the kingdoms of the world on the devil's terms and then announces the kingdom of heaven, God's own reign, arriving through his preaching and healing.
Jesus trusts the Father for bread, protection, and the kingdom rather than seizing them. The fishermen's immediate following shows faith as leaving the familiar to go with Jesus.

words.note: Peirazo, to test or tempt. The word can mean a test designed to prove someone's character or an enticement to sin, and both senses are present here. The Spirit leads Jesus into a testing that proves him faithful; the devil uses it to tempt him to fall.

Diabolos, the devil, from a Greek word meaning slanderer or accuser, used in the Greek Old Testament for the Hebrew satan, adversary. Matthew uses both names in this chapter. The devil is a personal enemy of God and his people, not merely a symbol for human evil.

Akoloutheo, to follow, go along behind, and so to be a disciple. It appears three times in this chapter, of the four fishermen and of the crowds. Following Jesus becomes one of Matthew's main words for discipleship.

Euangelion, gospel or good news. In the Roman world it could announce a victory or the birth or accession of an emperor. Isaiah had used the related verb for announcing God's reign (Isaiah 52:7). Jesus proclaims the good news that God's kingdom has come near.

christ: The temptation shows Jesus as the faithful Son who succeeds where Israel, and before it Adam, failed. Each reply comes from Moses' words to Israel: “Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (verse 4, quoting Deuteronomy 8:3); “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (verse 7, quoting Deuteronomy 6:16); “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (verse 10, quoting Deuteronomy 6:13). Jesus refuses to use his power for himself, to force God's hand, or to gain the world by bowing to evil, and he will refuse the same shortcut to glory at the cross, when he is again taunted with the words if You are the Son of God (27:40). Hebrews draws the pastoral point: he was tempted in every way as we are, yet was without sin, and so can sympathize with our weakness (Hebrews 4:15). The chapter's second half shows him as the light that dawns on those in darkness, beginning among the forgotten and the mixed population of Galilee.

hard.q: If Jesus was God, could he really have been tempted or have sinned?
hard.a: The New Testament insists both that Jesus was truly tempted and that he never sinned (Hebrews 4:15). Theologians have held two positions. Many argue that Jesus could not have sinned, because he was one person who was truly God, and God cannot sin; on this view the temptation was still real, since a temptation's force is felt most by the one who never gives in, and a wall under full pressure is tested even if it cannot fall. Others argue that Jesus, in his true humanity, was able to sin but did not, because a temptation that could not possibly succeed would not be the same kind of test we face. Both views affirm what the church confesses: that Jesus is fully God and fully human, that his temptation was genuine, and that his obedience was real and complete. The question of whether he could have sinned is a second-order one on which careful theologians have differed.

questions: Each temptation offered Jesus something good by the wrong means. Where are you tempted to reach for a good thing by a shortcut?
The devil quoted Scripture too. How can we tell the difference between using the Bible and obeying it?
The fishermen left their nets and their father. What would following Jesus require you to leave, loosen, or hold differently?
